title: Machine Code, Assembly, and High-Level Languages knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is the focus of the lesson “Machine Code, Assembly, and High-Level Languages”?
options: Machine Code, Assembly, and High-Level Languages
questions.answer_key: Machine Code, Assembly, and High-Level Languages
questions.explanation: The lesson focuses on Machine Code, Assembly, and High-Level Languages, within Computer Fundamentals and Development Environment. The example and subtopics anchor this concept in the C syllabus.

questions.prompt: Which approach best supports reliable work with machine code, assembly, and high-level languages?
options: Inspect the smallest example, validate assumptions, and test both ordinary and boundary cases.
Rely on one successful run and assume all platforms behave identically.
Disable compiler warnings so the output remains shorter.
Use raw memory operations without documenting object lifetime.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the smallest example, validate assumptions, and test both ordinary and boundary cases.
questions.explanation: A minimal reproducible example, checked assumptions, compiler diagnostics and boundary tests provide stronger evidence than a single happy-path run.

questions.prompt: When applying machine code, assembly, and high-level languages in a real C program, what should you do if the behavior is unclear?
options: Check the language/tool documentation, reduce the case, and record the observed result on the target compiler.
Guess based on how an unrelated programming language behaves.
Treat a compiler extension as portable ISO C without checking.
Continue even if input validity or object lifetime is unknown.
questions.answer_key: Check the language/tool documentation, reduce the case, and record the observed result on the target compiler.
questions.explanation: C portability depends on accurate language rules, toolchain support, and explicit assumptions; unknown behavior should be investigated rather than guessed.
